question.leadin: This man fought Huascar (WAHS-car) during the War of the Two Brothers.
question.text: Name this ruler who was strangled at the hands of Spanish conquistadors after converting to Christianity. He lost his capital of Cuzco to the Spanish when he failed to fill a room with gold.
question.clue: He offered to fill a large room with gold and silver for his ransom, but the Spaniards didn't release him.

swap.leadin: These people stored numerical information by using colored and knotted strings called quipus (KEE-poos).
swap.text: Name these people who also communicated using an extensive road network in the Andes called the "royal road" in Quechua (KEH-choo-uh). Their empire included sites like Machu Picchu (MAH-choo PEEK-choo) in modern-day Peru.
swap.clue: Descendants of this empire's royalty included Garcilaso de la Vega, and this empire was sometimes named for the four administrative suyus that it was divided into.

question.text: The Incas lived in this mountain range, in which they developed a series of bridges and roads to improve communication.
question.clue: A culture in this mountain range depicted a spider called the "Decapitator" and created a mummy known as the Lord of Sipan.

swap.text: This Incan "lost city" is believed to have been built for Pachacuti. It was re-discovered in 1911 by Hiram Bingham.
swap.clue: It is believed that it served as a retreat for Pachacuti Yupanqui, who had conquered the region of Tampu.

question.leadin: This country fought the Cenepa and Paquisha Wars against its northern neighbor, Ecuador.
question.text: Name this country, home to the cities of Arequipa and its capital, Lima.
question.clue: A culture from this country based in Sipan was known for pottery depicting exaggerated sexual acts, and another civilization in this country was known for geoglyphs depicting Condors and Herons.

swap.leadin: This term was originally used to describe the zipa chief of the Muisca people who would cover himself in gold and dive into Lake Guatavita.
swap.text: Name this term that was eventually used to describe an empire of gold sought by conquistadors.
swap.clue: During the first part of the journey in which Orellana travelled the length of the Amazon, a valley of Cinnamon and this place were the targets of Gonzalo Pizzaro.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about European relations with the New World FTPE.
question.text: The Incas fought a disastrous battle with this Spanish conquistador at Cajamarca in 1532.
question.clue: He led a band dubbed the "Famous 13" and gained over twenty tons of precious metals after setting up the "Ransom Room."

swap.text: This city was the capital of the Inca Empire. Pachacuti remodeled this city and expanded its holdings to form the Inca Empire.
swap.clue: A chief of this puma-shaped city adopted a name roughly translated as "world turner."

question.leadin: In the 1860s, ships from this country sailed to Polynesia to abduct laborers through a practice known as "blackbirding"
question.text: Name this country that needed workers for its profitable guano mines. A president of Japanese ancestry fought against the Shining Path in this country.
question.clue: Shining Path was opposed by this country's Grupo Colina death squad, which was overseen by its longtime autocratic president Alberto Fujimori.

swap.leadin: The artist Cecilia Vicuna often hangs artworks named for these objects from ceilings.
swap.text: Name these objects that were used for record-keeping and other purposes by the Inca.
swap.clue: This devices that were made of string and were commonly used for keeping census records or for monitoring taxes. The information on these devices was stored using knots.

question.leadin: Answer the following about remote sensing and the usage of aerial technology in archaeology.
question.text: While flying, Paul Kosok realized that what he believed were irrigation canals in a desert were actually animal-shaped lines, named for this civilization of southern Peru.
question.clue: Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche (RAI-keh) mapped structures created by these people.

swap.leadin: Early colonial writer Juan Freyle wrote an account of a ceremony in which a new ruler of these people was covered in gold dust and submerged in Lake Guatavita.
swap.text: Name this confederation of Northern Andean tribes that was led by co-rulers called Zipa and Zaque. They were encountered by the Conquistador Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada after his expedition sailed up the Magdalena.
swap.clue: This people, who mined salt in large gacha pots and imported gold for tunjo figures of humans or animals at Guatavita.

question.leadin: Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giraldez argue that, along with silver mined in Japan, the silver mined at this city generated the "birth of global trade" in a namesake economic cycle.
question.text: Name this Bolivian city whose Cerro Rico mine produced 80 percent of the world's silver between the 16th and 18th centuries.
question.clue: Workers in this city still give offerings to a goat-headed underworld deity called "The Uncle" or El Tio.

swap.leadin: These structures were first described as trail markers in the 1553 Cronicas del Peru by Pedro Cieza de Leon.
swap.text: Name these geoglyphs found in their namesake desert in southern Peru that include a hummingbird and spider. Some people think that aliens made these geoglyphs, as they can only be seen in full from above.
swap.clue: These things were damaged by Greenpeace activists wearing improper footwear as part of a 2014 protest.

question.leadin: Titu Cusi testified that the defeated leader at this battle threw a Bible offered by Friar Vincente de Valverde to the ground.
question.text: Name this battle in which the Inca leader Atahualpa was taken hostage.
question.clue: The losing side in this battle was engaged in a civil war against Huascar and was crippled by the decision to leave the bulk of its army outside the city walls.

swap.text: Evidence of geoglyphs suggested that the Amazon and Peru may have been home to powerful pre-Columbian civilizations. This Peruvian culture created geoglyphs in the desert that resemble spiders and hummingbirds.
swap.clue: This culture built the Cantalloc ("cahn-TAH-yoke")Aqueducts, exemplifying the corkscrew entrances of their puquios ("poo-KEE-ohʼs").

question.text: Under the "fictive reciprocity" of mit'a, laborers were supplied with large feasts and gifts of this substance. The sequestered aclla("AHK-yah"), or "chosen women," chewed maize to prepare this good for elite ceremonies.
question.clue: Chasquis runners carried this traditional fermented alcoholic beverage of the Inca. Women called aqlla lived in compounds their entire lives performing ceremonial tasks such as brewing this beverage.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about the Inca.
swap.text: This mandatory public service tax permitted 65 days for sufficiency farming, and divided the remainder of an ayllu's time for work between the temple and public works. Pizarro used it to enslave the Incan miners.
swap.clue: Las Casas would likely not have approved of the Spanish adoption of this Incan labor system which allowed them to conscript natives for public service work.

question.leadin: This ruler exempted Quechua speakers from taxation.
question.text: Name this son of Viracocha who defeated the Chanca invasion of Cuzco. The sun temple Coricancha, and possibly Machu Picchu, were built by this ruler.
question.clue: This ruler, who legendarily subjugated the (+) Chanka people with stone warriors, organized his realm into four suyus.

swap.leadin: Identify these much-regarded military commanders from South American history, FTPE.
swap.text: This huge badass burned Quito to the ground and killed its virgins to deny them to Pizarro's forces after losing the Battle of Mount Chimborazo to Belalcazar. Supposedly, he took the location of the Llanganatis Treasure to his grave, and with Quizquiz and Chalicuchima, commanded the Incan forces of Atahualpa.
